This line assigns `discount_applied` directly onto the instance inside `__init__`, so it behaves correctly and isn't part of the bug. The problem is specific to `items`, which never gets a matching per-instance assignment and instead falls back to the one list living on the class itself.
This blank line separates two method definitions and holds no logic that could cause carts to share items.

Calling `.append()` here is completely normal — mutating a list you're appending to isn't itself the mistake. The real defect is upstream: because `self.items` was never assigned in `__init__`, this call silently mutates the single list attribute owned by `ShoppingCart` itself rather than one belonging to `self`.

Setting `discount_applied` here works fine because it's a genuine per-instance assignment — this line isn't where carts leak items between each other. The actual bug is that `items` never gets assigned in `__init__`, so it keeps resolving to the one list attached to the class.
This blank line separates methods and contains no code relevant to the shared list.
This line only names the `total_items` method; the bug lives in how `items` was declared, not in this signature.

This line just reports the length of whatever `self.items` points to — it correctly reads the count, it just happens to be reading the class-wide shared list because no instance list was ever created. The defect is where `items` gets declared, not where its length is read.

This `[]` creates a brand-new local list every time `checkout_all` runs, which is completely different from `items = []` sitting in the class body and being shared by every instance. A fresh list literal inside a function is safe; the bug only happens when a mutable default lives on the class and gets mutated in place.

This appends a per-call receipt dict to a fresh local list, unrelated to how `ShoppingCart.items` ends up shared across instances.
This just reads the cart's `owner` attribute, a normal per-instance value with no shared-state problem.
